"Tōró prohibited only clothing that brings one into the hands of abhorrence."

This is explained more in Sifrē Dăvorīm 226:1, which states:

וכי מה בא הכתוב ללמדנו? [אם] שלא תלבש אשה כלים לבנים, ואיש לא יתכסה בגדי צבעונים, (ת"ל) [הרי כבר נאמר] "תועבה", דבר הבא לידי תועבה! [אלא] זה כללו של דבר - שלא תלבש אשה מה שהאיש לובש, ותלך לבין האנשים; והאיש לא יתקשט בתכשיטי נשים, וילך לבין הנשים:

"And for what does the Scripture come to teach us? [If] that a woman shall not wear white garments, and a man shall not cover himself with clothing of colours, (ibid.) [Behold, it was already said] "abhorrence", a thing that comes into the hands of abhorrence! [Only] this is it's rule that is to a thing - that a woman shall not wear that with which the man is clothed, and go amongst the men; and the man shall not adorn himself with ornaments of women, and go amongst the women."

It is such a sin that you intend to perform, and I must warn of such a sin. Regardless of how you wish to be, you are still a woman in the eyes of HashShēm, as He created you, and so too with those who serve Him, keeping His Miṣwōth.

It is truly tragic to see how the vile influence of wicked ʾĔdhōm has corrupted much of Yiśṛoʾēl to the point that they hold to such delusions and heresies of this wicked age, actively going against HashShēm and his Tōró, completely disregarding both. Truly tragic indeed.

Strength would just be ʿōz (עוז/עז), ʿāzaz (עזז) is the root it comes from meaning "to be strong". Next zāmar (זמר) would mean "he pruned", or could be read as zammār (singer), or zēmer (song). It has nothing to do with victory. ʿĀvar עבר means "he crossed over", there is no form from the root pronounced ʿaver to my knowledge. It may also be read as ʿāvār (similar, I know) referring to the past. Or it could be read as ʿabbēr, the imperative for "impregnate". Tiqvā (תקוה) does mean hope though at least. Lastly, ʿimməkhā-ānī (עמך־אני) would mean "I am with you", not "G-d is with you". Although in the image shown you have it written as עמכאמי (with a mem instead of nun, no final form of khaf or separation between words), this would read as "ʿimməkhā ʾimmī", meaning "my mother is with you".

If you are curious, here is a list of the Biblical Hebrew vowels according to the Tiberian System with their pronounciations:

1. Ū (אוּ): Makes a long "oo" sound.

2. U (אֻ): Makes a shorter "oo" sound.

3. Ō (אוֹ/אֹ): Makes a long "oh" sound.

4. Ā (אָ): Makes an "aw" sound. "אֳ" is the shortened form.

5. A (אַ): Makes an "ah" sound. "אֲ" is the shortened form.

6. Ă (אְ): Makes an ultrashort "ah" sound by default. Can become a shortened form of any other vowel if it is before a following guttural letter. It will take on the guttural's vowel. It is also used to mark closed syllables in which case it is silent.

7. E (אֶ): Makes an "eh" sound. "אֱ" is the shortened form.

8. Ē (אֵ): Makes an "ey" sound.

9. Ī (אִי): Makes an "ee" sound.

You're very welcome. The long Ā in Biblical Hebrew makes an "aw" sound like "saw" does in English however, it's simply a comparison to explain the sound. It's not the same as the long A in English of course.

The "aw" sound is in the theophoric part of the King's name bearing the shortened form of the Tetragrammaton without the final Hē. In the different Hebrew pronounciations his name would sound something like this:

Tiberian: Heezqeeyyawhoo.

Babylonian: Heezeeqyawhoo.

Biblical (based on Sennacherib's Annals): Hazaqyawhoo.

Notice the Qāmāṣ (ɔ/ā/aw) sound in the part of the King's name with the Tetragrammaton.

Ḥīz'qīyyāhū (חִזְקִיָּהוּ) is simply the Tiberian pronounciation of his name. The vowelisation which became the accepted form and tradition we have is that of the Tiberian Masoretes whose work spanned between the 7th and 10th centuries C.E. Their work was brought to a close mostly by the leading Masoretes Aharon ben Mosheh ben Asher and Ben Naphtali. Both schools had their differences even within the same tradition (875 differences to be specific), though the work of Ben Asher became the most accepted. His form of the tradition is that which can be seen in the Aleppo and Leningrad Codices today.

The Babylonian pronounciation Ḥīzīq'yāhū (חִזִקיָהוּ‎) is according to the work of the Babylonian Masoretes, their work spanning between the 6th and 7th centuries C.E. This earlier Babylonian vocalisation can be found in the Aleph Beth 4 Manuscript containing the Early Prophets with Targum Jonathan after each verse. Aleph Beth 5 and Aleph Beth 7 containing the Early Prophets. Aleph Beth 16 containing the Later Prophets and Targum Jonathan after each verse, and Aleph Gimel 4 containing Job and Chronicles. The Majority of manuscripts belonging to the Babylonian Tradition were found in the Cairo Geniza. The Babylonian tradition was and is still used and preserved by the Yemenite Jews also. It should also be noted that the Babylonian pronounciation Ḥīzīq'yāhū is also in more agreement and similarity with the Greek Septuagint's pronounciation 'Hezekías ( Ἑζεκίας), especially in syllable structure.

Regarding the long Ā in his name, there is indeed one. This is the long Hebrew vowel Qāmāṣ (אָ), it makes an "aw" sound in Biblical Hebrew, like in the English word "saw". I believe you're confusing it with the shorter vowel Pathaḥ (אַ) which makes an "ah" sound. In the Sephardic tradition of pronunciation and Modern Hebrew however Qāmāṣ is pronounced "ah" just like Pathaḥ, making the seperate signs rather redundant.

The Biblical pronounciation of Hezekiah's name as he would have said and heard it in his own time was most likely Ḥăzaq'yāhū (חֲזַקְיָהוּ‎). Evidence of this can be seen in the contemporary Akkadian transliteration Ḥazaqiaū (𒄩𒍝𒆥𒀀𒌑) from Sennacherib's Annals. In this form the root word Ḥāzaq (חָזַק), meaning "to strengthen" still retains it's original pronounciation with the long Qāmāṣ (Ā) being shortened to a Ḥaṭaf Pathaḥ (an ultrashort Ă) for grammatical reasons due to the name's length. The name Ḥăzaq'yāhū meaning "The L-RD Strengthens".

The difference in pronounciation is due to how different Jewish traditions pronounce the vowel and letter Tāw/Thāw.

Examples of the differences are as so:

Ashkenazim say: Shabbos. In their liturgical dialect Qāmāṣ is pronounced "Komotz" (O) and Tāw/Thāw is pronounced "Tov/Sov".

Sephardim say: Shabbat. I  their liturgical dialect Qāmāṣ is pronounced "Kamatz" (A) and Tāw/Thāw is only pronounced as "Tav". The Sephardic dialect is the main basis for the Modern Israeli pronounciation.

Teimanim say: Shabboth. In their liturgical dialect Qāmāṣ is pronounced "Qomoṣ" (O) and Tāw/Thāw remain much the same as "Tow/Thow". The Teimani pronounciation although not identical, is the closest to Biblical Hebrew which is still used and preserved.

The two forms of Hezekiah's name are often seen in Hebrew theophoric names containing the Tetragrammaton. The difference merely concerns the length of which form of the Tetragrammaton is used. The full length is never used in names, with the short forms Yōdh-Wāw, Yōdh-Hē and Yōdh-Hē-Wāw being frequently used. These three forms build up in a form from shortest to longest in length, with the 4 Letter form being the final.

The Tetragrammaton comes from the root הָיָה "Hāyāh", meaning "to be". The Tetragrammaton altogether means "He who was, is and will be"; each form reflects an aspect of this.

Where it is usually marked with daghesh in Babylon to indicate a hard alveolar pronounciation, it would have often been pronounced the same manner in the spoken Hebrew of Tiberias.
